clue.text: Playschool with several surfaces

parts.note: the play is Sheridan's The School for ..., and the missing word is gossip that keeps surfacing in that comedy

explanation.surface: A nursery with many different floor coverings.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Playschool' as 'play: School', Sheridan's comedy The School for Scandal, whose plot is a string of rumours coming to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's comedy is The School for Scandal, where gossip and disgrace keep coming to light.

clue.text: Scott's still here, it seems

parts.note: Paul Scott's novel title describes remaining in India after others leave, as if one is still here

explanation.surface: Someone named Scott apparently has not left yet.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott is Paul Scott, whose 1977 Booker-winning novel Staying On follows a British couple who remain in India after independence.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Scott's novel title means remaining behind, which is what being still here amounts to.

clue.text: Restless, getting shoddy stuff in exchange

indicators.note: the shoddy goods are placed in the middle of the word for exchange

parts.note: agio is the premium charged on currency exchange
tat is cheap shoddy goods

explanation.surface: Someone grows uneasy on being handed rubbish in a trade.
explanation.walkthrough: AGIO, the charge made for changing money, is a crossword staple; TAT goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitato is a musical direction meaning played in an agitated, unquiet manner.

clue.text: Duse his muse

parts.note: the actress Eleonora Duse was the lover and inspiration of an Italian poet and dramatist

explanation.surface: A man whose inspiration was the actress Duse.
explanation.walkthrough: Eleonora Duse, the great Italian actress, was the lover and leading lady of Gabriele D'Annunzio, who wrote plays for her.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriele D'Annunzio was the Italian writer whose plays and love affair centred on the actress Eleonora Duse.

annotationWithheld.clue: Lyrical timberwolf drowned in the Tagus War poet's Man's pursuit (3-7)

clue.text: Stimulus said to be given to post office by Count's foster-brother in Tennyson play

indicators.note: the word for a stimulus is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a fillip is a boost or stimulus

explanation.surface: A boost apparently handed to the post office by a character from a Tennyson drama.
explanation.walkthrough: In Tennyson's play The Falcon, Filippo is the foster-brother of Count Federigo.
explanation.definitionFit: Filippo is the Count's foster-brother and servant in Tennyson's verse play The Falcon.

clue.text: War poet's Man's pursuit

parts.note: Siegfried Sassoon's first memoir names its hero by his sporting pastime with hounds

explanation.surface: What a soldier-poet's chap went in for.
explanation.walkthrough: The war poet is Siegfried Sassoon, whose Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man is the first book of his fictionalised autobiography.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassoon's memoir is titled Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man, so riding to hounds is that man's pursuit.

clue.text: "…annointed sovereign of sighs and groans, / of all loiterers and malcontents" (Love's Labour's Lost)

definitions.text: "…annointed sovereign of sighs and groans, / of all loiterers and malcontents" (Love's Labour's Lost)

parts.words: "…annointed sovereign of sighs and groans, / of all loiterers and malcontents" (Love's Labour's Lost)
parts.note: Berowne's speech about Cupid has a gap before 'of all loiterers', to be filled with a word for a feudal lord

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Berowne describes Cupid as 'Th' anointed sovereign of sighs and groans, Liege of all loiterers and malcontents'; the missing word fills the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege is a feudal lord or sovereign, matching the run of royal titles Berowne gives Cupid.

clue.text: Browning's girl, saintly and repeatedly in peril?

definitions.meaning: Robert Browning's first published poem is named after a woman
the adjective for things belonging to Saint Paul, as in his epistles
the heroine of the silent film serial The Perils of ... was always in danger

explanation.surface: A poet's sweetheart who is both holy and always in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: Browning's poem Pauline; Pauline as the adjective of St Paul; and the heroine of the 1914 serial The Perils of Pauline.
explanation.definitionFit: Pauline is Browning's poem's addressee, the adjective for St Paul's writings, and the endangered heroine of a famous film serial.

clue.text: Thirties playwright somehow dotes on the stage

indicators.note: signals that the letters of dotes are to be rearranged in some fashion

explanation.surface: A dramatist of the 1930s is besotted with the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the stage' simply links, placing the playwright in the theatre; Clifford Odets wrote Waiting for Lefty and Awake and Sing! in the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: Clifford Odets was the leading American left-wing dramatist of the Depression decade.

clue.text: Strange, like Michael Moorcock's heat

definitions.meaning: Moorcock's 1972 novel opening his Dancers at the End of Time series has an adjective for foreign before Heat in its title

explanation.surface: Something odd, resembling the warmth in a Moorcock novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a fill-in: Michael Moorcock's 1972 novel is An Alien Heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Alien means foreign or unfamiliar, and it is also the adjective in Moorcock's title An Alien Heat.

clue.text: Composer of transcribed ex-"Hub" duet

indicators.note: music transcribed is rewritten in a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A musician credited with arranging a duet that once belonged to a group called the Hub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transcribed' rearranges EXHUBDUET into the name of Dieterich Buxtehude, the Baroque organist Bach walked miles to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Dieterich Buxtehude was a Danish-German Baroque organist and composer.

clue.text: High flier on Ludlum's agenda

definitions.meaning: the Greek youth who flew too near the sun on wax wings
Robert Ludlum wrote the thriller The ... Agenda

explanation.surface: An ambitious person appears in a thriller writer's plans.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Ludlum's 1988 thriller is The Icarus Agenda, so the name is literally on his agenda.
explanation.definitionFit: Icarus flew too high on wax wings, and his name heads Ludlum's thriller title The Icarus Agenda.

clue.text: Meditative emperor

parts.note: the Roman emperor who wrote the Stoic Meditations

explanation.surface: A thoughtful ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Aurelius was the Stoic Roman emperor whose private notebook is known as the Meditations.

clue.text: Jane Austen deployed its art convincingly

definitions.text: Jane Austen deployed its art convincingly

parts.words: Jane Austen deployed its art convincingly
parts.note: the art of convincing people is the title of Austen's last completed novel

explanation.surface: A novelist used a certain skill to good effect.
explanation.walkthrough: Austen's final completed novel shares its name with the art of convincing, so she literally deployed it.
explanation.definitionFit: Persuasion is both Austen's last finished novel and the art of winning someone over.

clue.text: Coarse sound of German satirist ()

indicators.note: says that a word for coarse is heard, not written

parts.note: gross means coarse or vulgar

explanation.surface: The rough voice of a German mocker.
explanation.walkthrough: George Grosz was a German artist whose savage caricatures satirised Weimar Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: George Grosz was a Berlin Dada artist known for biting caricatures of bourgeois society.

clue.text: Eaten pure, well cooked, it's like lyric poetry

indicators.note: cooking reworks ingredients, so the letters of eaten pure are rearranged

explanation.surface: Food consumed plain and properly prepared is pure poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Euterpe was the Muse of music and lyric poetry; the adjective describes things belonging to her.
explanation.definitionFit: Euterpe is the Muse of lyric verse, so the adjective formed from her name means relating to that kind of poetry.

clue.text: May a student of Jeffrey Wainwright have been in Conan Doyle's league?

definitions.text: May a student of Jeffrey Wainwright have been in Conan Doyle's league?

parts.words: May a student of Jeffrey Wainwright have been in Conan Doyle's league?
parts.note: Wainwright's poetry collection is The ... Pupil, and the Sherlock Holmes story is The ... League, sharing a hair-colour word

explanation.surface: Could someone taught by a particular poet have joined a Sherlock Holmes society?
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Wainwright's 1994 collection is The Red-Headed Pupil; Conan Doyle's Holmes story is The Red-Headed League.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginger-haired describes both Wainwright's pupil and the members of Conan Doyle's fictional league.

clue.text: Individual encountered by Hughes Mearns?

parts.note: Mearns's poem Antigonish describes meeting on the stair a man who wasn't there

explanation.surface: Somebody a particular poet ran into.
explanation.walkthrough: Hughes Mearns wrote 'Yesterday, upon the stair, / I met a man who wasn't there'; a man who isn't there is no one at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who does not exist, like Mearns's absent man on the stair, is a nobody in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Scottish peak painter

parts.note: a Scottish mountain is a Ben, and Ben is the forename of a British abstract painter

explanation.surface: An artist who paints Highland summits.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a landscape painter of mountains, but 'Scottish peak' gives his first name, Ben, as in Ben Nevis: the painter is Ben Nicholson.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Nicholson was a leading British abstract painter, and Ben is the Scots word for a mountain.

clue.text: Relay team associate, we hear, at resting place of Sir John Moore

definitions.text: resting place of Sir John Moore

indicators.note: signals that a word for a relay teammate is to be listened to

parts.note: a fellow runner in a relay is a co-runner

explanation.surface: A fellow sprinter, apparently, at the grave of a British general.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir John Moore fell at the Battle of Corunna in 1809 and was buried there, as Charles Wolfe's famous poem records.
explanation.definitionFit: Moore was killed defending the Spanish port of Corunna and buried on its ramparts.

clue.text: Australian storyteller begins dramatic yarns, some oddly naturalistic ()

indicators.note: the beginnings of the five words that follow are taken

explanation.surface: An Australian writer opens with theatrical tales, some strangely true to life.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Dyson was an Australian writer of bush and city stories around 1900.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Dyson was an Australian short-story writer and journalist of the Bulletin era.

clue.text: Spicy provisions for ancient Greeks in battle

definitions.meaning: the sea fight of 480 BC where the Greeks defeated the Persian fleet

explanation.surface: Seasoned food supplies for Greek soldiers in the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Salamis is the island off Athens where the Greek fleet beat Xerxes in 480 BC.
explanation.definitionFit: Salamis are spiced sausages, and Salamis is the naval battle the ancient Greeks won against Persia.

clue.text: Forster's eminent barrister who occasioned a notable climbdown

definitions.text: Forster's eminent barrister who occasioned a notable climbdown

parts.words: Forster's eminent barrister who occasioned a notable climbdown
parts.note: in A Passage to India a famous Indian lawyer arrives for Aziz's defence, and the case collapses

explanation.surface: A distinguished lawyer from a novel who forced someone to back down.
explanation.walkthrough: In A Passage to India the celebrated Calcutta barrister Amritrao defends Aziz; the case collapses when Adela withdraws her charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Amritrao is the eminent Calcutta lawyer brought in to defend Aziz in Forster's A Passage to India.

clue.text: Macedonian musketeer?

definitions.meaning: the holy mountain on a peninsula in Greek Macedonia

explanation.surface: A soldier from northern Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Mount Athos is the monastic peninsula in Greek Macedonia; Athos is also one of the Three Musketeers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Athos stands in Macedonia, and Athos is one of the three musketeers in Dumas's novel.

clue.text: His last case better remembered than his first ()

definitions.text: His last case better remembered than his first

parts.words: His last case better remembered than his first
parts.note: E. C. Bentley's detective appears in a famous last case and a later, lesser-known first one

explanation.surface: A detective whose final investigation is more famous than his debut.
explanation.walkthrough: E. C. Bentley's Trent's Last Case (1913) is a classic; the sequel Trent Intervenes and Trent's Own Case are far less known.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Trent is Bentley's detective, famous from Trent's Last Case rather than the stories that followed.

clue.text: A Barsetshire Lady

parts.note: a titled woman from Trollope's novels of the fictional county

explanation.surface: A noblewoman from Trollope's county.
explanation.walkthrough: Barsetshire is Anthony Trollope's fictional English county, the setting of his six Barchester novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Leslie is the surname of a titled lady among the gentry of Trollope's Barsetshire novels.

clue.text: Two articles defining Ms Musgrave

parts.note: the is the definite article
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A pair of grammatical words describe a particular woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Thea Musgrave is the Scottish composer of the opera Mary, Queen of Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Thea Musgrave is a Scottish-born composer, so her first name completes the title.

clue.text: Composer of vocal works hid them in disarray

indicators.note: describes the words hid them in being thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A songwriter concealed his scores in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Hindemith was the German composer of the song cycle Das Marienleben and much other vocal music.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Hindemith wrote operas and song cycles such as Das Marienleben among his works.

clue.text: French writer observed in Russian parliaments

definitions.meaning: Alexandre, author of The Three Musketeers
the plural of the name for the Russian legislative assembly

explanation.surface: A Parisian author is spotted among the Moscow assemblies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duma is the Russian parliament, so more than one gives the novelist's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandre Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers, and dumas are Russian legislative assemblies.

clue.text: Sunburn acquired in open-air fight by Greek of warrior caste?

indicators.note: the sunburn piece stands by, that is after, the word for fight

parts.note: to spar is to fight
a tan is the bronzing the skin gets outdoors

explanation.surface: Someone from a soldiering class got sunburnt at an outdoor bout.
explanation.walkthrough: Spartans were the Greek citizens of Sparta, raised entirely for war; the question mark marks the definition as loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Citizens of Sparta formed a hereditary class trained solely as soldiers.

clue.text: Thackeray presented a novel view of this poet and dramatist

definitions.text: Thackeray presented a novel view of this poet and dramatist

parts.words: Thackeray presented a novel view of this poet and dramatist
parts.note: the essayist who wrote Cato appears as a character in Thackeray's Henry Esmond

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist portrayed an earlier writer in fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel view' is literal: Joseph Addison, essayist and author of the tragedy Cato, appears as a character in Thackeray's novel Henry Esmond.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Addison, poet and author of the play Cato, is portrayed as a character in Thackeray's Henry Esmond.
